6.2. Gradient-based optimization

In order to solve for (6.1), one uses iterative optimization algorithms, including gradient descent and its variants, to find a local minimum of the objective function. In each step, the parameter vector 𝜽\bm{\theta} is adjusted in the direction opposite to the gradient of the function at the current point, as the gradient points in the direction of the steepest ascent. The update rule can be expressed as

(6.4) 𝜽(t+1)=𝜽(t)−η​∇𝜽ℓF𝜽(t).\bm{\theta}^{(t+1)}=\bm{\theta}^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\ell_{F_{\bm{\theta}^{(t)}}}.

The tuning parameter η\eta is referred to as the learning rate of the optimization process. In practice, the value of η\eta is crucial as it determines how big a step is taken on each iteration. If η\eta is too small, the algorithm may take too long to converge; if it is too large, the algorithm may overshoot the minimum or fail to converge.

For a polynomial neural network p𝐰p_{\mathbf{w}} with weights 𝐰=(W1,W2,…,WL)\mathbf{w}=(W_{1},W_{2},\ldots,W_{L}), at time step tt, each WiW_{i} is updated by

(6.5) Wi(t+1)=Wi(t)−η​∇Wiℓp𝐰(t)W_{i}^{(t+1)}=W_{i}^{(t)}-\eta\nabla_{W_{i}}\ell_{p_{\mathbf{w}^{(t)}}}

where ∇Wiℓp𝐰(t)\nabla_{W_{i}}\ell_{p_{\mathbf{w}^{(t)}}} is computed efficiently by backpropagation. In subsection 6.4, we explain the backpropagation algorithm, which can potentially find its applications in algebraic statistics beyond the neural network settings.

6.3. Connecting the learning degree to empirical observations.

We consider a polynomial neural network with architecture 𝐝=(2,2,3)\mathbf{d}=(2,2,3) and r=2r=2. We generate 5000 random datasets each consisting of 50 input-output pairs (𝐱,𝐲)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) where 𝐱=(x1,x2)∈ℝ2\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} and 𝐲=(y1,y2,y3)∈ℝ3\mathbf{y}=(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}. For each data pair, x1x_{1} and x2x_{2} are sampled uniformly from [−1,1][-1,1]. For γ=1,2,3\gamma=1,2,3, each coordinate yγy_{\gamma} is a homogeneous polynomial of degree two in two variables x1x_{1}, x2x_{2}, i.e.,

yγ=cγ,1​x12+cγ,2​x1​x2+cγ,3​x22.y_{\gamma}=c_{\gamma,1}x_{1}^{2}+c_{\gamma,2}x_{1}x_{2}+c_{\gamma,3}x_{2}^{2}.

For γ=1,2,3\gamma=1,2,3 and j=1,2,3j=1,2,3, we draw cγ,jc_{\gamma,j} from a standard normal distribution. We initialize the parameters randomly for each dataset and run gradient descent optimization of the mean squared error (MSE) loss with a learning rate of 0.010.01, and decaying by 0.90.9 for every 2,0002,000 training epochs. We stop training at a maximum of 20,000{20,000} epochs, and consider the neural networks whose gradient norm satisfies ‖∇ℓ‖2≤10−5\|\nabla\ell\|^{2}\leq 10^{-5} at the end of training. Instances whose gradient norm does not fall below the threshold within 20,000{20,000} iterations are discarded. The final functions learned by the neural networks satisfying the above criteria are approximately critical points. We recover the quadratic coefficients of the function learned by the neural network on each dataset from its weights at epoch 20,000{20,000} as follows:

For each output unit j=1,2,3j=1,2,3,

c1​j′\displaystyle c_{1j}^{\prime} =w2​j​1​w1112+w2​j​2​w1212,\displaystyle=w_{2j1}w_{111}^{2}+w_{2j2}w_{121}^{2},
c2​j′\displaystyle c_{2j}^{\prime} =2​(w2​j​1​w111​w112+w2​j​2​w121​w122),\displaystyle=2(w_{2j1}w_{111}w_{112}+w_{2j2}w_{121}w_{122}),
c3​j′\displaystyle c_{3j}^{\prime} =w2​j​1​w1122+w2​j​2​w1222.\displaystyle=w_{2j1}w_{112}^{2}+w_{2j2}w_{122}^{2}.

To assess the distinct functions learned by the neural network, we set tol=0.1\texttt{tol}=0.1, and consider two solutions are distinct if there exists γ=1,2,3\gamma=1,2,3 and j=1,2,3j=1,2,3 such that

|cγ​j′−cγ​j′¯|≥tol|c_{\gamma j}^{\prime}-\overline{c_{\gamma j}^{\prime}}|\geq\texttt{tol}

where cγ​j′c_{\gamma j}^{\prime} and cγ​j′¯\overline{c_{\gamma j}^{\prime}} are corresponding coefficients of the function learned by the neural network by the datasets.

For the architecture 𝐝=(2,2,3)\mathbf{d}=(2,2,3) and r=2r=2, out of the 5,0005,000 datasets, 27132713 reached the gradient norm threshold within 20,00020,000 training epochs. Based on the criteria for the coefficients of the final output, we learned 22 distinct functions whose coefficients differ by the tolerance threshold. We sort the distinct functions by descending the number of training nets it corresponds to. For the top three functions (Function 11, 22 and 33) learned by the architecture, they correspond to 1,5571,557, 560560, and 241241 datasets, respectively. In the figure below, we evaluate Function 11 (green), Function 22 (red), and Function 33 (yellow) against the ground truth (blue) on the three coordinates y1y_{1}, y2y_{2}, y3y_{3} separately.

The experiment shows that the three most frequently learned functions all align with the ground truth on the y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} coordinates, and being slightly off on y3y_{3}. Note that following the formula in 6.4, the learning degree of the architecture 𝐝=(2,2,3)\mathbf{d}=(2,2,3) and r=2r=2 is 3939, which provides an upper bound on the number of distinct functions the gradient descent algorithm is able to learn under proper conditions. The experiment implementation is available at [KLW24].

6.4. Backpropagation

To compute the gradient of the loss function efficiently one uses the backpropagation algorithm. Since Werbos introduced this algorithm in his 1974 PhD thesis [Wer74], backpropagation lies at the heart of modern successes in deep learning. For the computational algebraic geometer backpropagation is of interest as it provides a way to compute Jacobians of a parameter map Ψ𝐝,r\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r} exponentially faster than by naïve differentiation. We give a brief overview of the backpropagation algorithm following [Nie15, Chapter 2] and explain how it can be used to compute Jacobian ranks.

Let ℓ\ell be a loss function (e.g., as in (6.3)) satisfying the following assumptions:

  1. (1)

    ℓ\ell is smooth;

  2. (2)

    ℓ\ell can be written as a sum of loss functions ℓ=∑j=1Nℓ𝐱^j\ell=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\ell_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{j}}, where each ℓ𝐱^j\ell_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{j}} depends only on the sample 𝐱^j\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{j};

  3. (3)

    ℓ\ell depends only on the output of the network p𝐰​(𝐱)p_{\mathbf{w}}(\mathbf{x}), not on the state of intermediate layers; the training data f⁡(𝐱^j)f(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{j}) are considered as parameters.

Backpropagation provides a way to compute the gradient ∇𝐰ℓ​(𝐱^1,…,𝐱^N)\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}\ell(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1},\dots,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N}) efficiently. Note that in particular, if ℓ𝐱^\ell_{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} is just the network F𝜽​(𝐱^)F_{\bm{\theta}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) itself, this gives an algorithm for computing the gradient ∇𝐰F𝜽​(𝐱^)\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}F_{\bm{\theta}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}).

Let zjlz^{l}_{j} denote the input into the jthj^{\text{th}} neuron of the lthl^{\text{th}} layer. The error δjl\delta^{l}_{j} of this neuron is defined as

δjl≔∂ℓ∂zjl.\delta^{l}_{j}\coloneqq\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z^{l}_{j}}.
Theorem 6.7 ([Nie15]).

Let ajla^{l}_{j} be the output of the jthj^{\text{th}} neuron in the lthl^{\text{th}} layer, and let LL denote the last layer of the network. Then the following equations hold:

δjL=∂ℓ∂ajL​σL,j′​(zjL),δjl=σl,j′​(zjl)​∑k=1dlwl+1,j,k​δkl+1,∂ℓ∂wl,j,k=akl−1​δjl.\delta^{L}_{j}=\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a^{L}_{j}}\sigma^{\prime}_{L,j}(z_{j}^{L}),\quad\delta^{l}_{j}=\sigma^{\prime}_{l,j}(z^{l}_{j})\sum_{k=1}^{d_{l}}w_{l+1,j,k}\delta^{l+1}_{k},\quad\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial w_{l,j,k}}=a^{l-1}_{k}\delta^{l}_{j}.
Proof.

These are simple consequences of applying the chain rule. ∎

These equations give rise to Algorithm 1 below. The idea is to first compute the outputs of each neuron ajla^{l}_{j} via a “forward” run through the network and then compute the errors δjl\delta^{l}_{j} using the first two equations of Theorem 6.7 running “backwards” through the network. Finally, the gradient can be computed using the third equation from Theorem 6.7.

If we choose the loss function ℓ\ell to be the network F𝜽F_{\bm{\theta}} itself, backpropagation returns the gradient ∇𝐰F𝜽​(𝐱^)\nabla_{\mathbf{w}}F_{\bm{\theta}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). However, when we are interested in computing the Jacobian of Ψ𝐝,r\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r}, we need to compute the partial derivatives ∂wj,k,lcI(i)\partial_{w_{j,k,l}}c^{(i)}_{I}, whereas

(6.6) ∂F𝜽(i)∂wj,k,l​(𝐱^)=∑I∂cI(i)∂wj,k,l​𝐱^I.\frac{\partial F_{\bm{\theta}}^{(i)}}{\partial w_{j,k,l}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}})=\sum_{I}\frac{\partial c^{(i)}_{I}}{\partial w_{j,k,l}}\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{I}.

By choosing N≔(rL−1+d0−1d0−1)N\coloneqq\binom{r^{L-1}+d_{0}-1}{d_{0}-1} many samples 𝐱^1,𝐱^2,…,𝐱^N\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{2},\dots,\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{N} and applying backpropagation to each of them, we obtain a linear system from (6.6) in the unknowns ∂cI(i)∂wj,k,l\frac{\partial c^{(i)}_{I}}{\partial w_{j,k,l}}. For a generic choice of samples, this system has a unique solution and we obtain the Jacobian JΨ𝐝,rJ_{\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r}}.

This routine allows us to compute Jacobians and in particular the dimension of the neurovariety exponentially faster than via the naïve method of computing all derivatives of the parametrization Ψ𝐝,r\Psi_{\mathbf{d},r}. It can be easily adapted for computations over finite fields which makes dimension computations even faster. In [KTB19] this routine has already been implemented, however, their implementation contains a mistake in the set-up of the linear system described above. We provide a corrected implementation at [KLW24].

6.5. Case study: Linear Neural Networks

In addition to static properties of neural network optimization, we are also interested in the trajectory of practical optimization algorithms. This problem presents a more complex challenge, particularly in its general form. Limited results are known for the special subfamily of polynomial neural networks with activation degree r=1r=1. In this subsection, we survey prior results on the trajectory of the gradient descent algorithms applied to linear neural networks from literature in the algebraic statistics and machine learning communities separately. An interesting open question is to extend the analysis to polynomial neural networks with general activation degrees.

Linear neural networks are a special class of polynomial neural networks with the activation function ρ1​(𝐱)=𝐱\rho_{1}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}. The associated map from the set of parameters to vectors of homogeneous polynomials of degree one in d0d_{0} many variables is given by

Ψ𝐝,1:ℝd0×d1×⋯×ℝdL−1×dL→(Sym1(ℝd0))dL,𝐰↦p𝐰=[p𝐰(1)p𝐰(dL)].\Psi_{\mathbf{d},1}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times d_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{L-1}\times d_{L}}\rightarrow(\Sym_{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}}))^{d_{L}},\quad\mathbf{w}\mapsto p_{\mathbf{w}}=\begin{bmatrix}p_{\mathbf{w}}^{(1)}\\ \vdots\\ p_{\mathbf{w}}^{(d_{L})}\end{bmatrix}.

The neuromanifold for the architecture 𝐝\mathbf{d} is

ℳ𝐝,1={M∈ℝd0×dL∣rk⁡(M)≤min⁡{d0,d1,…,dL}}.\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{d},1}=\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times d_{L}}\mid\rk(M)\leq\min\{d_{0},d_{1},\ldots,d_{L}\}\}.

Note that in the linear case the neuromanifold is always equal to the neurovariety.

We denote the map from ℝd0×⋯×dL\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times\cdots\times d_{L}} to ℝd0×dL\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times d_{L}} as

μ𝐝(W1,W2,…,WL)=WL⋯W2W1.\mu_{\mathbf{d}}(W_{1},W_{2},\ldots,W_{L})=W_{L}\cdots W_{2}W_{1}.
Proposition 6.8 ([TKB19, Theorem 4]).

Let d~=min⁡(𝐝)\tilde{d}=\min(\mathbf{d}), 𝐰=(W1,…,WL)\mathbf{w}=(W_{1},\ldots,W_{L}) and W¯=μ𝐝​(𝐰)\overline{W}=\mu_{\mathbf{d}}(\mathbf{w}).

  • •

    (Filling case) If d~=min⁡{d0,dL}\tilde{d}=\min\{d_{0},d_{L}\}, the differential d​μd​(𝐰)d\mu_{d}(\mathbf{w}) has maximal rank equal to dim(ℳ𝐝,1)=d0​dL\dim(\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{d},1})=d_{0}d_{L} if and only if for any i∈[L−1]i\in[L-1], either rk⁡(Wj)=dL\rk(W_{j})=d_{L} for all j>ij>i or rk⁡(Wj)=d0\rk(W_{j})=d_{0} for all j<i+1j<i+1.

  • •

    (Non-filling case) If d~<min⁡{d0,dL}\tilde{d}<\min\{d_{0},d_{L}\}, the differential d​μd​(𝐰)d\mu_{d}(\mathbf{w}) has maximal rank equal to dim(ℳ𝐝,1)=d~​(d0+dL−d~)\dim(\mathcal{M}_{\mathbf{d},1})=\tilde{d}(d_{0}+d_{L}-\tilde{d}) if and only if rk⁡(W¯)=d~\rk(\overline{W})=\tilde{d}.

Besides static properties of the loss landscape, in the realm of neural networks, optimization often focuses on devising and refining algorithms to efficiently find the best model parameters that minimize a loss function. Key aspects of optimization include developing and analyzing optimization algorithms like gradient descent and its variants, understanding the impact of different loss functions, and ensuring model generalization through regularization. Additionally, researchers delve into convergence analysis to assess how and when algorithms reach optimal solutions. Since neural networks are, in general, complex models, the loss landscape is often non-convex, resulting in a significant risk of converging to a suboptimal local minimum. Analyzing the convergence trajectory is one of the most challenging problems in machine learning theory. We recall results on the convergence trajectory of deep linear neural networks with respect to ℓ2\ell_{2} loss in Theorem 6.9. This analysis provides crucial insights into the efficiency and effectiveness of how learning algorithms perform on these architectures.

Theorem 6.9 ([ACGH18, Theorem 1], informal).

Consider training deep linear neural networks with ℓ2\ell_{2} loss using the gradient descent algorithm. Assume that at initialization, the weight matrices are well-conditioned. In addition, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that at any time step TT,

(6.7) ‖Wj+1T​Wj+1−Wj​WjT‖F≤δ,\|W_{j+1}^{T}W_{j+1}-W_{j}W_{j}^{T}\|_{F}\leq\delta,

for all j=1,2,…,L−1j=1,2,\ldots,L-1. For any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, with a sufficiently small learning rate, there exists T0T_{0} such that the loss is no greater than ϵ\epsilon for any T≥T0T\geq T_{0}.

Theorem 6.9 shows that, when minimizing the ℓ2\ell_{2} loss for a deep linear network over a dataset with zero mean and unit variance, gradient descent converges to the global minimum at a linear rate, given mild assumptions. Similar results have been shown for deep linear neural networks with losses beyond the ℓ2\ell_{2} loss. In [BPAM23], the authors consider deep linear neural networks trained with the Bures–Wasserstein distance, a loss function commonly used in generative models. They analyze not only the critical points of the loss landscape but also the convergence of both gradient flow and gradient descent for the Bures–Wasserstein loss.

The convergence trajectory of polynomial neural networks with activation degree r≥2r\geq 2 remains an open problem. Heuristically, having a higher degree of activation reduces the symmetry in the parameter space, which may lead to interesting geometric properties in the trajectory of various optimization algorithms. We aim to establish theoretical guarantees for the convergence of general polynomial neural networks in our future work.
